tasks.description: Implement the Singleton pattern: a `Config` class where only one instance can ever be created.
tasks.hint:
Override `__new__`: `def __new__(cls): if not hasattr(cls, '_instance'): cls._instance = super().__new__(cls); return cls._instance`
Every call to `Config()` returns the SAME object.
Check: `c1 = Config(); c2 = Config(); print(c1 is c2)` → True
tasks.walkthrough:
`__new__` is responsible for creating the object. The first call builds one and stores it on the class; every later call returns that same stored object.
`c1 is c2` is True because both names point at the one instance. The settings dictionary is set up inside the guard so it isn't reset on later calls.

tasks.description: Implement the Observer pattern: an `EventEmitter` class where listeners register for events and get notified when events fire.
tasks.hint:
`self.listeners = {}` — a dict mapping event names to lists of callbacks.
`on(event, callback)` appends to the list.
`emit(event, data)` loops the list and calls each callback with data.
tasks.walkthrough:
`on` stores callbacks under an event name. `emit` looks up that name and calls each callback with the data.
Emitting an event nobody listens to, like logout here, simply does nothing thanks to the `.get(event, [])` default.

tasks.description: Implement the Factory pattern: a `ShapeFactory.create(type)` class method that returns Circle, Square, or Triangle instances.
tasks.hint:
`@classmethod def create(cls, shape_type): shapes = {'circle': Circle, 'square': Square}; return shapes[shape_type]()`
This decouples the caller from knowing which class to instantiate.
Add error handling for unknown shape types.
tasks.walkthrough:
The registry maps a string to a class. `create` looks the string up, and if it finds a class, calls it to make an instance.
Unknown names raise a clear ValueError rather than a confusing KeyError.

tasks.description: Implement a simple Strategy pattern: a `Sorter` class that accepts a sorting strategy (bubble, quick) and uses it.
tasks.hint:
Pass the strategy as a function: `sorter = Sorter(strategy=bubble_sort)`
The `Sorter.sort(data)` method calls `self.strategy(data)`.
You can swap strategies at runtime: `sorter.strategy = quick_sort`
tasks.walkthrough:
Both sort functions take a list and return a sorted copy, so either can be plugged into `Sorter`.
The `Sorter` doesn't know or care which algorithm it holds. Swapping strategies is just assigning a different function.

tasks.description: Implement the Decorator pattern (not Python @decorator — the OOP pattern): wrap a `Coffee` object with `MilkDecorator` to add milk cost and description.
tasks.hint:
Both base class and decorators implement the same interface (e.g., `cost()` and `description()`).
`class MilkDecorator: def __init__(self, coffee): self._coffee = coffee`
`def cost(self): return self._coffee.cost() + 0.50`
tasks.walkthrough:
Each decorator holds the object it wraps and forwards calls to it, adding its own cost and description on the way.
Because the decorators have the same methods as Coffee, they can be stacked in any order and used wherever a Coffee is expected.

lesson.intro:
Design patterns are named solutions to problems that come up again and again
in object-oriented code. Knowing the names helps you read other people's code
and talk about your own. Today: five of the common ones, each in a few lines
of Python.

sections.heading: Singleton: only one instance, ever
sections.body:
Override `__new__`, the method that creates the object before `__init__`
runs. If an instance already exists, return it instead of making another.
Useful for configuration and shared connections.

sections.heading: Observer: notify whoever is listening
sections.body:
An emitter keeps a dictionary of event name to list of callbacks.
`on` registers a callback; `emit` calls every callback for that event.
It's how buttons, web sockets and many frameworks work.

sections.heading: Factory: build the right class from a name
sections.body:
A dictionary from name to class, and a method that looks up and calls
the class. The caller says "circle" and gets a Circle without importing
or knowing about the class itself.

sections.heading: Strategy: swap the algorithm at runtime
sections.body:
Pass a function in and call it later. Because functions are values, the
strategy pattern in Python is barely a pattern at all.

sections.heading: Decorator (the pattern, not the @)
sections.body:
Wrap an object in another object with the same interface, adding
behaviour on the way through. A coffee with milk is a coffee that costs
a bit more and describes itself differently, but you use it the same way.
sections.code:
class Coffee:
    def cost(self): return 2.0
    def description(self): return 'Coffee'

class MilkDecorator:
    def __init__(self, coffee): self._coffee = coffee
    def cost(self): return self._coffee.cost() + 0.5
    def description(self): return self._coffee.description() + ', milk'

c = MilkDecorator(Coffee())
print(c.description(), c.cost())

watch_out: In a singleton, `__init__` still runs on every `Config()` call. Keep it empty or guard it.
`setdefault(event, [])` returns the existing list or creates one, so the append always has somewhere to go.
A factory dictionary holds the classes themselves (`Circle`), not instances (`Circle()`).
Decorator objects must expose the same methods as the thing they wrap, or code that used the original breaks.
